Exploratory Data Analysis: refined petroleum imports of landlocked economies¶

Thesis: Probabilistic Forecasting of Petroleum Imports and Supply-Shortfall Risk: Evidence from Kyrgyzstan and Other Landlocked Economies

This notebook examines the validated research datasets in data/research/ (dataset version 1.0.0, Comtrade snapshot 2026-11-02) before any model is fitted. It has four goals:

  1. Describe the data: structure, integrity, coverage and missingness.
  2. Characterise the forecasting target: distribution, trend, seasonality, persistence, stationarity and volatility of monthly import mass.
  3. Examine Kyrgyzstan in detail, then compare it with the rest of the panel.
  4. Screen the candidate predictors: supplier concentration, prices, exchange rates, inflation and geopolitical risk. The modelling implications are listed at the end.

It is descriptive only. No target value is interpolated or imputed, and missing months stay missing. Statistics that need an unbroken series (STL, ACF, unit-root tests) use the longest gap-free stretch.

def longest_stretch(s):
    # Longest run of consecutive non-missing months; s is indexed by month
    s = s.sort_index()
    ok = np.append(s.notna().to_numpy(), False)
    best, start = (0, 0), None
    for i, v in enumerate(ok):
        if v and start is None:
            start = i
        elif not v and start is not None:
            if i - start > best[1] - best[0]:
                best = (start, i)
            start = None
    return s.iloc[best[0]:best[1]]


def robust_sd(x):
    x = pd.Series(x).dropna()
    return 1.4826 * (x - x.median()).abs().median()

Observations. The target table is a complete rectangular grid: every country × product series has all 140 months from January 2015 to August 2026, and no key is duplicated. Missingness is never hidden: a month has a target value exactly when its data_status is observed, and every other month carries an explicit reason. There are no negative masses or values, and the bilateral table contains no World aggregate rows, so partner shares can be computed directly.

Most missing months are structural, not random. outside_reporting_span means the country does not publish monthly Comtrade data for that period at all, either before its first or after its last release. no_record_in_published_month means the country published the month but filed nothing under that HS line. Missing targets come almost entirely from these two causes, which reflect which countries report, not measurement noise. Removing mass with the unit-value check (mass_rejected_by_check) affects well under 2% of months.

2.2 Quality tiers and the modelling panel¶

The pipeline assigns each country-product series a tier (rules in config/settings.yaml). The analysis below uses Tier 1 + Tier 2 series of the two forecasting targets, gasoline and distillates including blends, which is the training pool of the thesis.

# Gap structure inside the panel: lengths of runs of consecutive missing months between observations
def gap_lengths(s):
    s = s.sort_index()
    first, last = s.first_valid_index(), s.last_valid_index()
    miss = s.loc[first:last].isna().astype(int).to_numpy()
    runs, n = [], 0
    for v in miss:
        if v:
            n += 1
        elif n:
            runs.append(n); n = 0
    return runs

gaps = []
for (iso, prod), s in panel.groupby(["iso3", "product_group"]):
    gaps += [(iso, prod, r) for r in gap_lengths(s.set_index("month").import_mass_t)]
gaps = pd.DataFrame(gaps, columns=["iso3", "product_group", "gap_months"])
print(f"Internal gaps in the panel: {len(gaps)}; series with no internal gap: "
      f"{panel_keys.shape[0] - gaps[['iso3', 'product_group']].drop_duplicates().shape[0]} of {panel_keys.shape[0]}")

Observations, Section 2.

  • The status map shows three reporting regimes. Tier 1 countries report almost every month. Tier 2 countries start late (Uzbekistan from 2019), stop early (Rwanda after 2022, Laos, Zambia and Burkina Faso after 2023-24) or have long interruptions (Kazakhstan 2024, Laos 2021, Burundi 2015 and 2024). Tier 3 countries report rarely or not at all, including Tajikistan and Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan's Central Asian neighbours. Missing data therefore cluster by country and by time, so a panel model has to handle ragged edges, with series that end at different months. Only 12 of 22 gasoline series reach mid-2026.
  • Inside the panel, 18 of 44 series have no internal gap. Of the 54 internal gaps, 46 last only one or two months. The remaining 8 gaps of 10-13 months are all in Tier 2 series (Kazakhstan, Laos, Burundi). Masking missing months in the loss function is enough, and imputation is not needed.
  • Value, unit value and release date are complete whenever the target is observed, and supplier fields are 99% complete. hhi_12m needs 6 observed months in its window, so it is missing at series starts (95% complete). export_mass_t is missing in 29% of months, mostly because no export was recorded, so it should not be used as a feature without care.

3. Distribution of the target¶

The target is monthly import mass in tonnes (import_mass_t). Series differ in scale by two orders of magnitude, so per-series summary statistics come first, followed by the shape of the distribution before and after a log transform.

In [9]:
def describe_series(s):
    x = s.dropna()
    return pd.Series({"n": len(x), "mean_kt": x.mean() / 1e3, "median_kt": x.median() / 1e3, "sd_kt": x.std() / 1e3,
                      "cv": x.std() / x.mean(), "min_kt": x.min() / 1e3, "max_kt": x.max() / 1e3,
                      "skew_raw": stats.skew(x), "skew_log": stats.skew(np.log(x[x > 0])),
                      "kurt_raw": stats.kurtosis(x), "kurt_log": stats.kurtosis(np.log(x[x > 0]))})

desc = (panel.groupby(["product_group", "iso3"]).import_mass_t.apply(describe_series).unstack()
        .join(panel_keys.set_index(["product_group", "iso3"])[["quality_tier"]]))

Observations, Section 3.

  • Scale differs by two orders of magnitude: median monthly imports range from 1.9 kt (Andorra gasoline) to 406 kt (Swiss distillates). Pooled models need per-series scaling, and absolute error metrics would be dominated by the largest countries, so scaled metrics (MASE, scaled CRPS) are needed.
  • Variability is high: the median coefficient of variation is 0.37 for gasoline and 0.33 for distillates, and above 0.9 for Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan.
  • In tonnes, most series are right-skewed (median skewness 0.6). A log transform removes the upper tail but reverses the skew (median -0.5 for gasoline, -0.8 for distillates): it exposes a lower tail of collapse months. The log is still the right working scale, because it makes errors proportional and stabilises variance. The lower tail is what the thesis cares about, because those months are supply shortfalls.
  • After per-series robust standardisation, 3.2% of panel months lie beyond 3 robust SDs and 2.0% beyond 4, against 0.27% and 0.006% under a normal distribution. The extreme months are almost all on the low side, and the most extreme are near-zero months (Armenia, Aug-Sep 2015, under 1 tonne; Burundi, 2016), which look like partial reporting, not real supply. Gaussian intervals would be badly too narrow in the lower tail, which supports quantile, conformal or Student-t intervals, plus robust losses for training.
  • Kyrgyzstan is a mid-sized importer of gasoline (median 42 kt a month, CV 0.40), the sixth-largest gasoline series in the panel.

4.2 Seasonality¶

In [15]:
def seasonal_index(s):
    # Month / mean of its calendar year, full years only (12 observed months)
    d = s.dropna().to_frame("m")
    d["year"], d["mon"] = d.index.year, d.index.month
    full = d.groupby("year").m.transform("count") == 12
    d = d[full]
    d["idx"] = d.m / d.groupby("year").m.transform("mean")
    return d

for ax, prod, color in zip(axes, ["gasoline", "middle_incl_blends"], [BLUE, ORANGE]):
    d = seasonal_index(kg_series(prod)[0])
    groups = [d[d.mon == m].idx for m in range(1, 13)]
    h, p = stats.kruskal(*groups)
    kw_rows.append({"product": SHORT[prod], "full_years": d.year.nunique(), "H": h, "p_value": p,
                    "peak_month": d.groupby("mon").idx.median().idxmax(), "trough_month": d.groupby("mon").idx.median().idxmin(),
                    "peak_index": d.groupby("mon").idx.median().max(), "trough_index": d.groupby("mon").idx.median().min()})
    bp = ax.boxplot(groups, tick_labels=list("JFMAMJJASOND"), patch_artist=True, widths=.6,
                    medianprops={"color": INK}, flierprops={"markersize": 3})

# STL decomposition of log gasoline on the longest gap-free stretch
fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 2, figsize=(13, 8), sharex="col")
strength = []
for col, (prod, color) in enumerate(zip(["gasoline", "middle_incl_blends"], [BLUE, ORANGE])):
    st = longest_stretch(np.log(kg_series(prod)[0]))
    st.index = pd.DatetimeIndex(st.index).to_period("M").to_timestamp()
    res = STL(st.asfreq("MS"), period=12, robust=True).fit()
    var = lambda x: np.var(x, ddof=1)
    f_s = max(0, 1 - var(res.resid) / var(res.seasonal + res.resid))
    f_t = max(0, 1 - var(res.resid) / var(res.trend + res.resid))
    strength.append({"product": SHORT[prod], "stretch": f"{st.index.min():%Y-%m} to {st.index.max():%Y-%m}",
                     "months": len(st), "seasonal_strength": f_s, "trend_strength": f_t})
    for ax, comp, name in zip(axes[:, col], [st, res.trend, res.seasonal, res.resid],
                              ["log mass", "trend", "seasonal", "remainder"]):
        ax.plot(comp.index, comp.values, color=color if name != "remainder" else MUTED, lw=1.3)
        ax.set_title(f"{SHORT[prod]}: {name}" if name == "log mass" else name, fontsize=9.5)
        ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
for ax in axes[-1]:
    ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.YearLocator())
    ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%Y"))
save(fig, "eda07_kyrgyz_stl")

product stretch months seasonal_strength trend_strength
0 Gasoline 2019-11 to 2026-05 79 0.350 0.090
1 Distillates 2022-03 to 2026-05 51 0.590 0.630

Seasonal and trend strength follow Wang, Smith and Hyndman (2006): $F = \max(0, 1 - \mathrm{Var}(R)/\mathrm{Var}(X + R))$ on a 0 to 1 scale. Values below about 0.4 mean the component explains little beyond noise.

In [18]:
def unit_root(x):
    x = pd.Series(x).dropna()
    adf_p = adfuller(x, autolag="AIC")[1]
    kpss_p = kpss(x, regression="c", nlags="auto")[1]
    verdict = ("stationary" if adf_p < .05 and kpss_p > .05 else
               "unit root" if adf_p >= .05 and kpss_p <= .05 else "inconclusive")
    return adf_p, kpss_p, verdict

rows = []
for prod in ["gasoline", "middle_incl_blends", "lpg"]:
    st = longest_stretch(np.log(kg_series(prod)[0]))
    for name, x in [("log level", st), ("first difference", st.diff()), ("seasonal difference (12)", st.diff(12))]:
        a, k, v = unit_root(x)
        rows.append({"product": SHORT[prod], "transform": name, "n": int(x.notna().sum()),
                     "ADF p (H0: unit root)": a, "KPSS p (H0: stationary)": k, "verdict": v})
display(pd.DataFrame(rows).round(3))
product transform n ADF p (H0: unit root) KPSS p (H0: stationary) verdict
0 Gasoline log level 79 0.000 0.100 stationary
1 Gasoline first difference 78 0.000 0.100 stationary
2 Gasoline seasonal difference (12) 67 0.000 0.100 stationary
3 Distillates log level 51 0.002 0.017 inconclusive
4 Distillates first difference 50 0.000 0.100 stationary
5 Distillates seasonal difference (12) 39 0.998 0.100 inconclusive
6 LPG log level 79 0.000 0.010 inconclusive
7 LPG first difference 78 0.000 0.100 stationary
8 LPG seasonal difference (12) 67 0.000 0.100 stationary

KPSS p-values are bounded to the interval [0.01, 0.10] by its lookup table. "Stationary" means ADF rejects a unit root and KPSS does not reject stationarity. "Unit root" means the reverse. "Inconclusive" means the two tests disagree, which is common with about 100 monthly points and level shifts.

Observations, Section 4 (Kyrgyzstan).

  • Level and trend. Gasoline imports fluctuate strongly from month to month (8 to 92 kt) around a stable level of about 40-50 kt. The 12-month mean stays within 31-55 kt for the whole period, and annual totals for full years range from 486 to 642 kt with no persistent trend. Distillates shift upward from 2024 (895 kt in 2024 and 1,080 kt in 2025, against 500-820 kt before), so a model has to absorb a level shift, through a short training window or a break indicator. LPG grows steadily, from 15 kt to 142 kt a year.
  • The 2025 shock is visible: gasoline fell to 8-27 kt a month in Jul-Nov 2025, the longest low run in the record, and recovered in Dec 2025. 2025-2026 values are first releases and probably revised upward later (data_quality_report.csv, issue V01), so the depth of the fall is uncertain. The Dec 2025 distillate spike (194 kt) is the largest month in the record and may be a stock-building response.
  • Seasonality. Kyrgyz gasoline has a significant month effect (Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.004): its median peak is December (1.46 of the annual mean) and its trough September (0.66). Seasonal strength on the 79-month gap-free stretch is still only moderate (0.35). Distillates have no significant monthly pattern (p = 0.11). Their higher STL seasonal strength comes from a 51-month stretch with an upward trend, and is not reliable. Calendar features matter for gasoline and are secondary for distillates.
  • Persistence. For gasoline, the ACF has one significant spike at lag 1 (about 0.33) and then falls inside the confidence band, and the PACF cuts off after lag 1. The series behaves like a noisy, mean-reverting process, close to AR(1) around a slowly moving level. Distillates are more persistent (ACF significant at lags 1-2, then slow decay), consistent with the level shift. Short autoregressive lags (1-3) and rolling means are the most promising lag features.
  • Stationarity. Log gasoline is stationary on both ADF and KPSS. Distillates and LPG are inconclusive in levels because of their trends, and stationary after first differencing. Models that work in levels, such as tree models on log mass, need a trend or level feature for distillates.
  • Prices. The import unit value follows Brent closely in levels (correlation of logs 0.78), much less in monthly changes (0.27), and monthly mass is unrelated to unit value (Spearman 0.01). Price is a deflator and context variable, not a demand driver at this frequency. The unit value relative to crude rose from about 1.0 in 2015-2024 to 1.21 in 2025-2026, consistent with a supply squeeze.
  • Suppliers. Russia supplied 77-99% of Kyrgyz gasoline by mass in every year. Kazakhstan is the main alternative, with Belarus appearing in 2025. Distillates are diversifying: Russia's share was 77-94% in 2020-2024 and fell to 65% in 2025 and 60% in 2026, while Kazakhstan's rose to about 30-35%. Distillates were also diversified in 2016 (Russia 54%). Gasoline concentration stays very high (12-month HHI median 0.89), so HHI varies little over time for Kyrgyz gasoline. It is likely to help more as a cross-country feature in a pooled model. Months with a low Russia share cluster in 2018-2020 and 2025, but they are not systematically weak import months (Spearman with YoY mass change -0.07, p = 0.46, Section 6).

5. Cross-country comparison¶

5.1 Scale per person and volatility¶

Observations, Section 5.

  • Volatility falls with income and import scale. The calmest series belong to European importers (Switzerland, North Macedonia, Czechia, Slovakia; robust SD of monthly log change about 0.12-0.20). The most volatile belong to Central Asian, Caucasian and low-income importers (Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Bolivia, Zambia, Uzbekistan, Burundi; 0.45-0.85). Kyrgyzstan is more volatile than the panel median: 0.39 against 0.32 for gasoline (rank 14 of 22, where 1 is the calmest), and 0.38 against 0.27 for distillates (rank 16 of 22). Its imports per person are close to the panel median (73 kg of gasoline and 96 kg of distillates a year).
  • Luxembourg and Andorra import 5-30 times the panel median per person (fuel tourism and transit sales), a reminder that imports are not consumption and that the panel is heterogeneous.
  • Seasonality is country-specific. Only 10 of 22 gasoline series have a significant month effect. Profiles differ in timing: European series peak in summer (North Macedonia, Andorra, Luxembourg in Jul-Aug), while Kyrgyzstan, Bolivia and Laos peak in December, and Uzbekistan in May. A pooled model should learn seasonality per series, for example with country-specific month effects, and not as one panel-wide profile.
  • Stationarity varies. In log levels only 6 of 22 gasoline and 4 of 22 distillate series are clearly stationary; the rest are inconclusive or have a unit root. After one difference, 43 of 44 series are stationary. No series needs more than one difference.
  • Countries hardly co-move: the median cross-country correlation of year-on-year log changes among Tier 1 series is 0.06 for both products. Pooling can help by sharing dynamics (how a series reverts after a shock), but there is little shared shock signal to borrow. Within a country, gasoline and distillates co-move moderately (median about 0.35; Kyrgyzstan 0.42), which supports shared features across a country's two products.

6. Supplier concentration across the panel¶

The Herfindahl-Hirschman index is $\mathrm{HHI}_t = \sum_j s_{jt}^2$, where $s_{jt}$ is supplier $j$'s share of import mass. It equals 1 for a single supplier and $1/N$ for $N$ equal suppliers. The 12-month pooled version is used, because monthly shares are noisy.

Spearman correlation across countries, median HHI vs volatility: rho = -0.06, p = 0.79, n = 22
Kyrgyz gasoline: Russia share vs YoY log change in mass: rho = -0.07, p = 0.461, n = 116

Observations, Section 6.

  • Concentration varies widely between countries: from diversified importers such as Burkina Faso, Bolivia and Hungary (median 12-month HHI 0.13-0.22) to near-single-supplier markets. Kyrgyzstan has the second-highest gasoline concentration in the panel (median HHI 0.89, after Moldova's 0.95 from Romania), with one of the highest Russia shares (median 96%).
  • Russia is the dominant gasoline supplier for five panel countries: Kyrgyzstan (96%), Kazakhstan (94%), Armenia (88%), Uzbekistan (74%) and Azerbaijan (39%). For them a single exporter's policy, such as the Russian export bans of 2023, 2024 and 2025, is a common risk factor, even though their monthly volumes barely co-move in normal times. This group could serve as the "shared supplier" feature for the supplier-graph hypothesis.
  • Concentration is not related to volatility across countries (Spearman -0.06, p = 0.79). Within Kyrgyzstan, months with a lower Russia share do not show weaker import growth (-0.07, p = 0.46). Concentration measures exposure to one supplier's decisions, not observed instability. Its predictive value, hypothesis H4, has to be tested in shock windows, not inferred from these averages.
  • The usual top supplier is often a trading hub, not a refiner: the UAE for Rwanda and Zambia, Singapore for Zimbabwe. So partner shares measure who sells, not necessarily the physical route.

Observations, Section 7.

  • Brent and WTI are almost perfectly collinear (0.99 in year-on-year changes), so only one belongs in a model. Global and Russia GPR are also closely related (0.76), and Brent is moderately linked to Russia GPR (0.51), mainly through the 2022 spike. The Kyrgyz som was stable for long periods, with step devaluations in 2015, 2020 and 2022, so the exchange-rate signal sits in a few episodes. Kyrgyz inflation peaked at about 15% in 2022-23.
  • Same-month and short-lead correlations with Kyrgyz import growth are small (|rho| < 0.2): Brent is weakly positive at leads of 0-2 months, and the exchange rate and CPI are near zero at every lead.
  • The strongest signal is a negative association with geopolitical risk 7-11 months earlier (rho about -0.3, nominal p about 0.001): import growth tends to be lower some 7-10 months after a rise in GPR. The robustness check gives different answers for the two products. For gasoline it survives, and even strengthens, when the 2022-23 war period is removed (rho -0.39 for global GPR and -0.35 for Russia GPR). For distillates it mostly disappears (-0.03 for global GPR; -0.21, p = 0.05, for Russia GPR), so it rested largely on that single episode. Overlapping year-on-year windows and about 65 tests per product make the nominal p-values far too optimistic. The gasoline result is a hypothesis worth testing in the ablation study (a lagged GPR feature), not a finding.
  • External indicators should enter as candidate features to be ablated, with low expectations for average accuracy. Their value, if any, is more likely to show in shock windows (2022, 2025) than in these full-sample averages.

8. Publication lag and data quality flags¶

A forecaster only knows a month's imports once the country publishes them. The publication lag (days from month end to first Comtrade release) therefore sets how many months behind the information set is.

Observations, Section 8.

  • Publication lags range from under a month to well over a year. Kyrgyzstan's median is 68 days, against a panel median of 86, so a one-month-ahead forecast made in real time is in effect a three-month-ahead forecast from the last known value. Eight panel countries (Andorra, Burundi, Burkina Faso, Kazakhstan, Laos, Rwanda, Zambia, Zimbabwe) have median lags above 180 days. They contribute training history but cannot serve as real-time predictors for their neighbours. In particular, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan's second supplier, publishes too late to help. Every feature must be lagged to its release date (as-of replay).
  • Quality flags are rare: about 1-2% of panel months have a mass outlier (|robust z| > 4), and rejected masses are under 1%. Outliers stay in the data on purpose, since many are real supply events. No Kyrgyz month is flagged as a mass outlier. About 15% of gasoline months and 34% of distillate months contain some mass that Comtrade marks as estimated, so mass quality varies with reporter practice.
  • The high-severity issues in data_quality_report.csv (first-release Kyrgyz data for 2025-26, the 2025 value gap, the 2015-17 mirror mismatch, misfiled HS lines) define the sensitivity analyses the thesis must run.

9. Summary of findings and modelling implications¶

# Finding Evidence Implication for modelling
1 Complete month grid with an explicit reason for every missing month; missingness is structural (who reports, and when) §1, §2.1, Fig. eda01 Mask missing months in losses; never impute targets; handle ragged series ends
2 Panel of 44 Tier 1+2 series in 22 countries (5,549 obs.); 85% of internal gaps last 1-2 months §2.2 Enough for small global models, not for large deep nets
3 Median series level ranges from 1.9 to 406 kt; raw mass right-skewed; log mass left-skewed with a heavy lower tail (2% of months beyond 4 robust SD) §3, Fig. eda03-04 Model log mass with per-series scaling; scaled metrics (MASE, scaled CRPS); robust losses; non-Gaussian intervals
4 Kyrgyz gasoline: stable level, significant but moderate seasonality (Dec peak 1.46, Sep trough 0.66) §4.1-4.2 Calendar features for gasoline; strong naive baselines
5 Kyrgyz distillates: level shift from 2024, no significant seasonality; supplier diversification towards Kazakhstan in 2025-26 §4.1, §4.5 Break-aware training windows or level features for distillates
6 Short memory: gasoline close to AR(1) around a slowly moving level; log level stationary §4.3 Lag 1-3 and rolling-mean features
7 Unit value tracks Brent in levels (0.78), mass unrelated to unit value (0.01) §4.4 Use price as a deflator or context feature, not a key driver
8 Kyrgyz gasoline is the second most concentrated series in the panel (HHI 0.89, Russia 96%); concentration is unrelated to volatility §4.5, §6 HHI is mainly a cross-sectional feature; test H4 in shock windows
9 Kyrgyzstan is more volatile than the panel median; volatility is higher in low-income and Central Asian importers §5.1 Stratify evaluation by tier and country group
10 Seasonality differs across countries in timing and strength (10 of 22 significant); series barely co-move (median rho 0.06) §5.2, §5.4 Series-specific seasonality in pooled models; pooling helps through shared dynamics, not common shocks
11 External indicators: weak links; Brent and WTI collinear; lagged GPR is negatively linked to gasoline growth, robust to removing 2022-23 §7 One oil price and one GPR; test a 7-10 month GPR lag in the ablation study
12 Publication lag: Kyrgyzstan 68 days, panel median 86, eight countries over 180 §8 As-of replay with first_released; effective horizon = lag + forecast horizon
13 2025-2026 Kyrgyz data are first releases, likely revised upward §4.1, data_quality_report.csv Treat the depth of the recent shock as provisional; evaluate on data as first released

Overall. The data are clean, well documented and sufficient for the planned univariate-plus-covariates global forecasting design, with Kyrgyzstan as a credible case study. The EDA suggests that most predictive signal comes from the series' own recent history and calendar, and that supplier and macro covariates should be treated as hypotheses tested by ablation, not as assumed drivers. The heavy lower tail of the target and the structural breaks support probabilistic forecasts with robust, non-Gaussian uncertainty, which is the thesis approach.
